**2026-11-19.** **A data task can delete a store row** with `<q:store key="…" delete="true"/>`.
This adds an attribute to the frozen `q:` namespace (`urn:sutra:q:1.0`), which is why the release
is 0.7.0. The addition is backward compatible: existing packages load and run unchanged. **A
data-store row's revision now starts from the database clock,** so a row that is deleted and
created again never reuses a revision. **A message that correlates to no live instance is
recorded,** and a channel can send it to a process instead of refusing it. **The AMQP 1.0
transport works with IBM MQ.** **Codecs can seal what they send** and resolve secret references in
their own bundle files. One migration, V103, runs at first boot on PostgreSQL. There is no archive
or snapshot format change.

## Before you upgrade

**Check these against what you run:**

- **Rows created after the upgrade start from a large revision, not 1.** An insert into a data
  store now seeds `rev` with the database clock in microseconds since the epoch (about
  1.8 × 10^15 today); each write still adds 1. Rows written before the upgrade keep their
  revisions. Anything outside the engine that reads `rev` and assumes a new row is at 1, or that
  revisions are dense, must stop assuming it. The `rev` column must be a 64-bit integer (`BIGINT`),
  which every shipped migration declares. A typed store whose table you created yourself must
  declare it the same way.
- **V103 builds an index concurrently at first boot** (PostgreSQL, `alias_index_retired_lookup`, a
  partial index on the alias index). It blocks no writes and adds I/O in proportion to the alias
  index. A completing instance now writes one more alias-index entry per correlation key it
  retires.
- **A message that correlates to no instance is now a WARN log line and an audit record** (see
  below). A sender that keeps answering ended instances will show up in both. Before, an HTTP sender
  got a 500 and nothing else recorded it; the HTTP answer is unchanged.
- **A `local://` delivery for an instance that has ended takes the poison posture at once.** The
  refusal no longer carries `sutra.waitPending=true` when every instance that carried the key has
  ended, so it is not retried for about four minutes first.
- **Deployments that expect timer surges should run more than one shard** (`sutra.engine.shards`,
  `SUTRA_ENGINE_SHARDS`; default `1`). Unchanged since 0.6.25: due timers fire as fast as they fall
  due, and with one shard that work shares the single execution lane with new work.

## Deleting a data-store row (`q:` addition)

`<q:store key="…" delete="true"/>` on a data task's write removes the key's row. The data output
association needs no `<sourceRef>`. Deleting a missing key is a no-op.

| Form | Row present | Row missing |
|---|---|---|
| `delete="true"` | deleted | no-op |
| `delete="true" expect="unchanged"`, key read earlier | deleted while its revision is still the one read, else a conflict | a conflict (it is gone) |
| `delete="true" expect="unchanged"`, key never read or read missing | a conflict (it appeared) | no-op |

The conflict is `SUTRA.RUNTIME.DATASTORE.CONFLICT`, which an error boundary catches. A delete runs
where a write runs: on the `<bpmn:transaction>` scope's store transaction, else on its own. It
waits behind a `forUpdate` row lock and invalidates the read cache like a write. It works on
key/value and typed stores on PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB and SQL Server. `delete` with `field`,
`forUpdate`, `expect="absent"` or any key-query attribute, or a delete reference used as a read, is
refused at load with the new `SUTRA.PARSE.STORE.DELETE_INVALID` (`sutra lint`, sealing and deploy
alike).

Data-store SPI: `DataStore::delete_if_revision` and `DataStoreTx::delete_if_revision`, with a default
body (an unconditional delete that reports it applied), implemented by the in-memory store, the read
cache and the three SQL dialects.

## Revisions start from the database clock

Every insert used to seed `rev = 1`. Once a process can delete rows, a key can go from revision 1,
to deleted, to re-created at revision 1 with another value. Two things compare revisions and would
miss that: another replica's read cache would serve the old row, and an `expect="unchanged"` write
or delete that read the old row would apply. Now the insert reads the database's own clock in the
insert statement (so every replica shares one clock), never below 1. Revisions are strictly
increasing per row but not dense. The guarantee holds while the database clock moves forward: a
clock stepped backwards between a delete and the re-create can break it.

## A message no instance waits for

When a message on a channel a wait subscribes to finds no live instance carrying its correlation key
(`SUTRA.RUNTIME.RELAY.CORRELATION_NOT_FOUND`, a reply after its instance ended for example), the
engine now records it, on every transport:

- a WARN log line with `SUTRA.INBOUND.RELAY_UNCORRELATED`, naming the channel, the message type, the
  dedup key and the correlation keys looked for, never the body or the headers;
- an `inbound.RELAY_UNCORRELATED` record in the deployment's audit journal, with no instance id.

A key value is masked in both when its alias, or a variable its expression reads, is `sensitive`, or
when a redactor masks it.

`uncorrelated: { start: <processId> }` on an inbound channel in `channels.yaml` (no `q:` change)
sends such a message to that process instead of refusing it. The process's start events on the
channel are reserved for uncorrelated messages, and the instance reads `event.uncorrelated`
(`code`, `keys`, `ended`). A message that correlates still resumes its instance and starts nothing.
A malformed block fails to load; `sutra lint` reports a `start` that names no process of the
package, or one with no start event on the channel, as `SUTRA.CONFIG.CHANNEL.UNCORRELATED_INVALID`.

## IBM MQ over AMQP 1.0

The `amqp` transport is proven at tier 2 against two IBM MQ 10.0.1 queue managers: local queues, a
remote queue definition over a mutual-TLS channel pair, a topic with administrative subscriptions,
TLS and SASL PLAIN on the AMQP channel, concurrent sends, and a queue-manager restart. Two fixes
were needed for IBM MQ to work at all, and both apply to every broker:

- **Each connection now has its own container id.** The sink used one id for every send and the
  source one per channel. IBM MQ takes the container id as the client's identity and closes an open
  connection when another opens with the same id, so concurrent sends, and replicas of one channel,
  cut each other off.
- **The sink sets the message's `to` property** to the target address. IBM MQ refuses a message
  without it.

New options, all off by default so the wire is unchanged unless you set them:

- inbound `address-type: queue | topic` and destination `?type=queue|topic`, sent as the link's
  terminus capability (IBM MQ reads an address without one as a topic string);
- destination `durable`, `ttl-ms`, `body=text|binary` (stored by IBM MQ as `MQSTR` and
  `MQFMT_NONE`, where the default `data` section is stored as `MQAMQP`),
  `property-names=identifier` and `application-properties=none` (no MQRFH2 header for an IBM MQ
  application reading a default queue);
- the `x-amqp-message-id`, `x-amqp-correlation-id`, `x-amqp-reply-to` and `x-amqp-subject` headers,
  both ways;
- outage logging: `SUTRA.{INBOUND,OUTBOUND}.AMQP.OUTAGE_STARTED` when the broker is lost and
  `…_ENDED` when it is back, with `outage_started`, `outage_ended` and `outage_ms`.

Also changed: the sink sends the outbox key as `message-id`; the source renders a binary message id
that is not printable text as hex (it decoded it as UTF-8, so two binary ids could share an
idempotency key), drops trailing blanks from `reply-to` and `subject`, and treats an all-zero id as
none. A destination query value the sink cannot take is a permanent
`SUTRA.OUTBOUND.AMQP.CONFIG_INVALID`.

## Codec SPI: `seal` and `bind_refs`

Two default methods on `PayloadCodec` (`sutra-codec-spi`), inert unless a codec overrides them:

- `seal(body, content_type)`: the governing codec's last transform of an outbound message, after
  its read-back passed and before the outbox commit, for `<q:send>` and both forms of reply
  (template renders included). `Ok(Some(bytes))` replaces the body; an error refuses the message
  with `SUTRA.OUTBOUND.SEAL_FAILED`. This lets an extension codec sign messages.
- `bind_refs(resolver)`: called once when a deployment's bundle codec is planned on the runtime
  host, with the engine's reference resolver (`env:`, `secret:`, `vault:`, `${…}`), so a codec's
  bundle files can name secrets as references. An error refuses the deployment with
  `SUTRA.CODEC.BIND_REFS_FAILED`.

Plus `InboundChain::seal_outbound` beside `validate_outbound`, and `CodecRefResolver`. Existing
codecs are unchanged. The engine still names no format and no algorithm.

## Fixed

- **A deployment flip could serve an older set of versions, or route a channel to a version whose
  lanes were not built yet** (database deployment source). The deploy API, the
  `LISTEN sutra_deployments` loop and the quiescence sweep re-activated the served set without
  mutual exclusion, so one flip could land between another's lane rebuild and its transport rewire:
  a request for the new version's channel answered 404 (`RESOLVE.CHANNEL.UNKNOWN`), or a broadcast
  briefly had one subscriber. Re-activations are now serialized and each reads the store afresh.
- **`make image` could ship another tree's engine code** when several trees were built on one host:
  the Dockerfile's shared cargo target cache and a reused `COPY` layer's file times let cargo take
  changed crates as fresh. Freshness is now decided by content. Published images were built from a
  cold cache and are not affected.
